summary:
American Samoa's own criminal code does not punish consensual sodomy. The first sodomy statute, enacted in 1963, covered male homosexual and heterosexual conduct and did not address lesbian conduct; the Fono's 1979 revision, effective in 1980, retained prohibition only for public acts, prostitution, conduct involving minors and conduct with persons unable to consent. The age of consent is 16, regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Same-sex marriage is not licensed. On 20 March 2003 the Senate rejected a bill introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster that would have outlawed it, after the House Judiciary Committee recommended the bill be killed; at the committee hearing fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that fa'afafine do not seek marriage with men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing. In July 2015 Attorney General Talauega Eleasalo Ale was reviewing whether the United States Supreme Court's 2015 marriage-equality ruling reached the territory and said he did not know, while the Governor stated that it did not apply, citing the territory's preamble, its constitution, Christian values and its unorganised and unincorporated political status. No same-sex couple had filed an application at that point, and a 2026 law-review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa records that none has applied since.

In January 2016 the Senate unanimously confirmed former Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as a District Court judge after he told confirming senators, including retired High Court associate judge Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, that he had not read the 2015 ruling, that the district court does not deal with it, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change.

In July 2024 an on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, tested whether the territory's ban would survive a challenge under the Fourteenth Amendment. As of mid-2024 the ban is treated locally as operative and its constitutional durability as an open question. The 2026 article reaches the opposite conclusion on the law, holding that the 2015 ruling does apply despite those official statements and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; it sets out a litigation path through the High Court of American Samoa first, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, then the United States Department of the Interior. Since 13 December 2022 the territory has been obliged to recognise, though not perform, same-sex marriages performed legally in another jurisdiction, with equal treatment for same-sex and opposite-sex couples.

The territory's marriage code does not specify the sex of the parties. It refers to the age of 'the male' and 'the female' on a form in which parties identify as 'son' and as 'daughter'.

Gender markers on local documents are changeable within limits. The High Court of American Samoa has held that birth certificates may be altered only to correct information that was erroneous at the time of recordation or to reflect a name change due to adoption, and the Office of Vital Statistics reads that ruling as covering applications from transgender people: it changes the name on a birth certificate when presented with a name change order, and may change the gender marker with medical documentation of the sex change.

Documented trans-specific legal matters in the territory concern employment and criminal proceedings. In June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity, and in September 2023 the United States Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teenager; that charge is the most recent documented instance of violence against a trans person in this record, no later instance is documented, and no outcome for the charge is stated.

Public climate combines cultural recognition with religious conservatism. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in Samoan scholarship as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival was held in August 2016 in Utulei, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community draw family support. Society is nonetheless highly religious, conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate, and open displays of affection between couples, same-sex or opposite-sex, may offend. A 2009 travel column described reserved public behaviour as expected of people of all orientations in the territory.
tangentialFactors:
In July 2015 American Samoa was the only United States territory that had not settled whether the federal marriage-equality ruling applied to it, while Puerto Rico, the United States Virgin Islands, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it; the territory's Attorney General said applicability was still under review and that he did not know. That comparison is dated 10 July 2015 and describes the position at that time.

The 2003 bill's defeat means the territory deliberately declined to enact a formal same-sex marriage ban before the 2015 ruling, and the committee record preserves contemporaneous fa'afafine testimony opposing such a ban on religious grounds rather than on grounds of marriage rights.

A 2009 travel column contrasted the territory with Fiji, describing homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture while noting that reserved public behaviour is expected, and reported that hotels in Pago Pago skew toward business travel. The column is a publication's own framing and is now more than fifteen years old.

The 2026 law-review article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative here, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality of an untested statute book. No court in the territory has decided the question.
localsOnly:
The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, and re-anchored its identity to cultural pride. It campaigns for the community and runs annual events; the first Pride festival took place in August 2016 in Utulei with pageant, song, dance and poetry competitions, and beauty pageants among the fa'afafine community draw family support in numbers.

Residents have obtained relief in the employment sphere: a June 2023 federal civil action alleged a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's suit against the territorial government, and in September 2023 the United States Justice Department settled an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee with the American Samoa Government.

Residents seeking to amend a birth certificate deal with the Office of Vital Statistics, which changes the name when presented with a name change order and may change the gender marker on medical documentation of the sex change, reading the High Court's ruling to cover transgender applications even though the ruling itself addresses only erroneous information and adoption-related name changes.

The territory's own legislative and academic record is active on the marriage question: the Fono rejected a ban in 2003, a constitutional law professor surveyed the community in July 2024, and local attorneys published the 2026 analysis. Fa'afafine are described in Samoan scholarship as an integral part of traditional culture, and a long-standing practice of raising some boys to fill a domestic role is documented, alongside a highly religious society in which conservative attitudes on gender and sexuality dominate.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2015 federal marriage-equality ruling applies to American Samoa is unresolved in this record. The 2026 law-review article says it does and that a certificate would have to be issued; the territory's Governor and judiciary have acted on the premise that it does not. No court has ruled, and no same-sex couple is documented as having applied for a licence at any point.

No outcome is stated for the February 2023 sexual-abuse charge involving a 16-year-old transgender teenager, and no later instance of violence against a trans person is documented in this inventory. Whether further incidents occurred and were not recorded is not sourced either way.

No source in this inventory reports a refusal by the Office of Vital Statistics to change a gender marker, or any appeal from such a refusal, so the practical limits of the medical-documentation requirement are not sourced.

Federal passport policy and the 2025 executive orders on sex definition, healthcare funding and sports are not restated here; they are carried at the national level of the parent record. This summary covers only the territory's own laws, institutions and documented events.

No figure is available for the prevalence of discrimination complaints, police reporting, or public attitudes toward trans people in the territory; the 2024 survey tested constitutional durability, not incidence.
